principles.text: Avoid buying into strength when the broader market/tape is extended to the upside (e.g., after multiple consecutive gap-up days); wait for a pullback instead of chasing.

Want the sector or market to align with the individual stock before entering — prefers to see the sector ETF pull back into its own rising EMA/unfilled gap before buying a stock within that sector, rather than trading the stock in isolation.

Prefers a stock to close strong into a key intraday level (e.g., a 60-minute candle testing the 9 EMA / trendline) before entering; a weak-looking candle heading into its close is a reason to pass rather than anticipate the bounce.

When there is no real structure to place a stop against (e.g., a fast, gappy first-minute candle), use a fixed percentage stop (roughly 1.5-2.5%) instead of a structural one — accepting a lower win rate — rather than chasing a stock that has already extended too far past its breakout level.

A trading thesis or narrative (e.g., "if X's earnings are bad, money rotates to competitor Y") only matters once it's confirmed by actual market/price action — don't trust logic alone without checking how similar situations have played out historically and how the market is actually reacting.
Lowered average risk per trade from about 0.5% of account (prior year) to about 0.3% this year, and considers that reduction a good decision.

Rarely trims winning positions anymore; prefers to hold full size for at least two to three weeks when a stock is working, and has become progressively more comfortable holding larger positions over time rather than de-risking early.

Rarely moves a stop up to breakeven even after a stock has moved favorably; keeps the stop at the original entry-based level and, if he wants to lock in gains, manually exits rather than mechanically trailing the stop.

Typical position size is around 20-25% of account (rarely above 30%), with per-trade risk still held under ~0.3% by using tight technical stops (often under 1% from entry) rather than by cutting position size.

Avoids initiating shorts when market breadth is improving, even if a specific sector looks locally weak (rolling over from a declining 50 EMA) — breadth strength argues other areas will hold up and absorb any single-sector weakness.

After getting stopped out, deliberately stops trading for the rest of the day ("before I get tilted") rather than continuing to search for another entry — treats tilt risk as a hard stop condition, not just a feeling to push through.

Actively tracks his own condition/mood and will cut back on streaming (and by extension, trading) rather than force it when he's not feeling well or not in the right headspace, even taking planned days off.
